comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
BFD99E3510584CE288CFEDD104F27D27.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

F566C403FDD447249D7903C4D29728D8.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

A8DEB40992BD4616A76067705CCCCCCA.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

F9D88F00C48944C089EA331D5539B177.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

6ABDFD11F6984478B9ABA157F66C793A.description: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.

7E2AE95DE40549C6919A3DC7FF5B007A.description: Provide a conclusion that follows from the narrated experiences or events.

0818DA458C3443E08C2480303E75A233.description: Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, and description, to develop experiences, events, and/or characters.

7084ACA63D924A2488939DCF6BF32F7E.description: Engage and orient the reader by establishing a context and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally and logically.

A454A350B9D745B39F615310A49ABC6D.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences.

7BC40C397B144E229216B3B6702DFA52.description: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from the information or explanation presented.

4F30FCC566DD4D2695870CBF737D7A6B.description: Establish and maintain a formal style.

D36F6498A0684256938C05DD40A566AE.description: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.

D72FB5458935425CB38CE9C48F586D99.description: Use appropriate transitions to clarify the relationships among ideas and concepts.

F5F9DF7159C94BFEA750C630D9A663E2.description: Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.

813F9B8ED53D4861A008489D1DC88DBF.description: Introduce a topic; organize ideas, concepts, and information, using strategies such as definition, classification, comparison/contrast, and cause/effect; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., charts, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.

714D25DC184D4BC8A1020C87073FACA0.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content

91EB3DDDAAA04B11B3D47F72A1440AF6.description: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from the argument presented.

F8308EC007D34EB4BEED0A9E8984EB98.description: Introduce claim(s) and organize the reasons and evidence clearly.

1FDF185A711A4472BF0CB723BFF24805.description: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

63D45D7027004FBEB06C196F3AAA3FDD.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

1CB192E87C824D47A630B13FD8A35843.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

3DE97F0E0B584AA693B16854D9F4DD2A.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

12E60B0E43714038B6EB7CA40E14FB1D.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

6C57B84DA6A7426FB8955A42D223B26D.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

B083574273FB495AAF9F5A19962DC6A1.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

C885DFAC0CB94080AF40D8426AE9E8DA.description: By the end of grade 8, read and comprehend science/technical texts in the grades 6—8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

15B92FE2CF994D289901C7485DD46EFC.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

EE5DE4E28AD546429B98EE6C138B035E.description: Compare and contrast the information gained from experiments, simulations, video, or multimedia sources with that gained from reading a text on the same topic.

A7D508DD0E00414F9354B8C1FADD183A.description: Distinguish among facts, reasoned judgment based on research findings, and speculation in a text.

8D08D19FF6E44091B317B6D6CDAF354F.description: Integrate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text with a version of that information expressed visually (e.g., in a flowchart, diagram, model, graph, or table).

8A9C0FF5920540689726501015B7EB92.description: Analyze the author's purpose in providing an explanation, describing a procedure, or discussing an experiment in a text.

D0092B41A2EB41BFAE0F873FAA1D8046.description: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to an understanding of the topic.

5CB60DEB4181413C97041FA9FBCB609D.description: Determine the meaning of symbols, key terms, and other domain-specific words and phrases as they are used in a specific scientific or technical context relevant to grades 6—8 texts and topics.

08B7D66BE9B449DA9E79C96550FA4C64.description: Follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks.

8035895DF559492AA72BB7219C21D1AD.description: Determine the central ideas or conclusions of a text; provide an accurate summary of the text distinct from prior knowledge or opinions.

1B3ACB032638445A9C8D32E3354C6724.description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of science and technical texts.

AB7422C73CF040768A1C381CDCEA3000.description: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects 6—12

7523F4C182214466A4762F0BC560F290.description: By the end of grade 8, read and comprehend history/social studies texts in the grades 6—8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

A5FC91F3EFFC49B78436EB6C015625C4.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

0C2179C0F9E446C6AA65494029B8EAF0.description: Analyze the relationship between a primary and secondary source on the same topic.

BB51CCA1059D4D22A19F0C72BEFE23AF.description: Distinguish among fact, opinion, and reasoned judgment in a text.

2760B05578E24ECE85EBDD2989F1AD68.description: Integrate visual information (e.g., in charts, graphs, photographs, videos, or maps) with other information in print and digital texts.

7F58576AA0594765827568976F9E8A6B.description: Identify aspects of a text that reveal an author's point of view or purpose (e.g., loaded language, inclusion or avoidance of particular facts).

B872CD6865224CC989469A72A9D2687A.description: Describe how a text presents information (e.g., sequentially, comparatively, causally).

877DEB1D585C4B46BB18D97383C084CA.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including vocabulary specific to domains related to history/social studies.

051704D15FBB4C59BD4FE6686CC84CC1.description: Identify key steps in a text's description of a process related to history/social studies (e.g., how a bill becomes law, how interest rates are raised or lowered).

313B2390E38D474988370E68B5DB1400.description: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary of the source distinct from prior knowledge or opinions.

E350FF0C16684CC19A527B6AAE2AD8D3.description: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources.

C7636A646CEE42B895F27607AE2A9E96.description: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies 6—12

8CCCE99BB56647D0978D81BA899D6B26.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6—8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

E81EAE5B30414477AAA663F737BFD139.description: Describe how the media use propaganda, bias, and stereotyping to influence audiences.

03494F0F715A4AA6B25C7AB7F2221099.description: Distinguish between primary and secondary sources;

BD5812B74CDD4E67BC4BCC410481D3D6.description: Compare and contrast one author's presentation of events with that of another (e.g., a memoir written by and a biography on the same person).

F602F6429AFD4DCB9EDB25E0CF096C22.description: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.

FBE481DCAF704869A15DE8E44CC1D7D0.description: Integrate information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.

6D1517F8896942DC930558E3BD76CC25.description: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.

7965022324564C85BE1F6F938BD344F5.description: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.

7EC9A117917547C9AC15D720F2A01E38.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.

F3D676F59C2845F09EDF8AB061F22E54.description: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text (e.g., through examples or anecdotes).

98EDF39B1049482C9F4A632EB7D7D483.description: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.

6521621BBA08435DA044284C4A230CD8.description: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

B13CD020A9AB41D3B5CFEE9B2A612A15.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6—8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

25BC4BDCB2F64074A9171D1D0D9996A7.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

3B34CCF418D84148863454A52639FCA9.description: Compare and contrast texts in different forms or genres (e.g., stories and poems; historical novels and fantasy stories) in terms of their approaches to similar themes and topics.

9DBA0169878A43A4BEC7389F45D228AA.description: Compare and contrast the experience of reading a story, drama, or poem to listening to or viewing an audio, video, or live version of the text, including contrasting what they "see" and "hear" when reading the text to what they perceive when they listen or watch.

38609AB23F4D4611829FEBA2D9C4384A.description: Explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker in a text.

DB58EA2D3BFF41A69A4914BD9302F494.description: Analyze how a particular sentence, chapter, scene, or stanza fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the theme, setting, or plot.

4F586677921B4E118815A1417DAC544A.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.

D17A98D130394D36B2AF2CA663CDDFBC.description: Compare a cultural value as portrayed in literature with a personal belief or value.

B077769D7C554CBF81BD392020F83524.description: Analyze works of Hispanic and Native American text by showing how it reflects the heritage, traditions, attitudes, and beliefs of the author and how it applies to society;

750A8F6226A9419C8170C9B894501856.description: Analyze how a cultural work of literature, including oral tradition, draws on themes, patterns of events, or character types, and how the differing structure of the text contributes to society, past or present;

8FBC3ACAF87B450F8AB252D386A7BD6D.description: Describe how a particular story's or drama's plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.

37A1129E4D924261A5E3B4DE36D7993F.description: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.

01ABDD8D3A9D496BAE73AFB8D4E673E9.description: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

C532F575A1C748BD821212CDEFFC9C4F.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

B899332AADD64D23AF23111FAAABE3FB.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

6FA7B9396EA747E38A566B05BB0227D7.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

9741B75926A84928A7783D8441120EB7.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

3E777B9147364D9AA3D56376E0C502D3.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

5C9E722D464244F8A72C650D2D036FBF.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

83F1AFADF6F14760A13E6678C8F12241.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

C144FFA1087842D3A3DADF12BCBE4182.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

3093A0FD485A4412987ECBFF63230430.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

08928B3AF3124EED905E6C55B355B876.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

FD5D6D5E1DE1436E9E4C7DC276D31BFB.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

document.title: New Mexico Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

47B0552C39524E96BEB6F3D44C7ED762.description: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
comments: For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?

414F53F7366D423BAEEE09DD59A0A3A3.description: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

F098DEAC102349799B48BDDFC72F7907.description: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

FD3EC78F21554E4CBDF035D435E2904A.description: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

comments: For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies?
6B9A17E91822479E8BFC7AF4C145421D.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.

9E0089E31F9F48C094683B4FAD1635BC.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
comments: For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.

F6E5F7DB5BC240EF985AAC503C73F0D1.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

comments: For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.
562A12E250364916BA534D5F0916953B.description: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.

93E83AEED1974A99B3FFE0A7CDA6220E.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

0DF2D77E630447538B5215553BE63323.description: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.

904257AA3F4B4CAEBAC6E2AF71C1BBDD.description: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
comments: For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh-grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth-grade science book.

D4479A2DFC464D78BC3CF490F8BE2443.description: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
comments: For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.

BA3BF8370CCD40418449E7262D8729E0.description: Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

comments: For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.
F40E2B22308843EDA0C905D81E407A78.description: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.

AC632D8035E44959B9FFFCBBD49782DF.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

D1B74C7204CA40EBA94ED841B972E227.description: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population.

490FE669C0064DAA8ED7034075F37157.description: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
comments: For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.

ABF967E267A7472EB1B6D66102434879.description: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.
comments: For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

AB79688965494F5594A85550DBFD7570.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.

comments: For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.
BBD41EA55C0647FC85B0C69BB0D31549.description: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.

8F7F1712D4AD40829881EF82AFCD2AF0.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.

7BE0E6ED7C73416FBB850C60DBE80067.description: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related.
comments: For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."

1AEBB85588784070BA39431D03E73863.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

1F266484BA2A4192A304C440FD188F11.description: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

comments: Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.
4A89B724F69048E8BB09B2B6028FF832.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.

73D59B55162D47F7967EABEC129A59D6.description: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.

EA24942B9BAB4420BFE76B64F34406CA.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

B0BE7AA32C9D43E48301156193B897BB.description: Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

627A890D78F84901A76D9ABAEDE7622C.description: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

BAAD012309144B1681F871E68BEC3A25.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.

3F7198985ED942318E40267314263C6D.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.

AA34B5DB41CB469EA9469A7A19430125.description: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

F939533DABFB4446882E1EFC90356E86.description: Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

225CD910E06344CB9754D917E1B59C18.description: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.
comments: For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged.

DC4092B8B40C4A88A8792279D65D62FE.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.

767A5969A88C4D45875B70B5DEC3E2CD.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.

comments: Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
F2FEB5E17EDB45C897133922A228DE4B.description: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems.

D0E360CB97D64FA4BF40743D56C79A85.description: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

comments: For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn.

97933D86E67944A79110994A73FAABCF.description: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

818F0475C50A49FA852735017B783C3A.description: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.

D766B90619EC403AB5F149DFD79A616F.description: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

comments: For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction <sup>1/2</sup>/<sub>1/4</sub> miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.
2DF1E1F59FFE4A28AAC1DAC37D344D6E.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.

076BBB635BE14347BD28649BB0D6F1A4.description: Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

1C61DCBE546C4B6788AFA9FECFB8AE8E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

BBF30359CCD94DBDAFD9F8F48EB6106E.description: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.

DC9E078135494389BA80C428AC24D280.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
688AE77F5E494ADBA0224F08F5F8C82C.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
E2FA03691E6C4C329D0D196BF3A74EBE.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

B5928A7A05C846D38F69ECD7842F9270.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

37AF9A605CAE4F848ECD085EBC1B4B63.description: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

F9139EDA5A0E4E00934D4C836A2EDF7E.description: Understand vector subtraction v - w as v + (-w), where -w is the additive inverse of w, with the same magnitude as w and pointing in the opposite direction. Represent vector subtraction graphically by connecting the tips in the appropriate order, and perform vector subtraction component-wise.

09A3C4970ECF4A6CBAEFE8D0C77DD157.description: Given two vectors in magnitude and direction form, determine the magnitude and direction of their sum.

6641658B0FF34DEF95B5F51650EC60D1.description: Add vectors end-to-end, component-wise, and by the parallelogram rule. Understand that the magnitude of a sum of two vectors is typically not the sum of the magnitudes.

0636728B5DD94AF0B0012396B1F28DAF.description: (+) Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors.

DEC0C64987A449D88C8476CB26EE1740.description: (+) Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of an initial point from the coordinates of a terminal point.

FE60295F89934B2A889A5DFEDE120011.description: (+) Recognize vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction. Represent vector quantities by directed line segments, and use appropriate symbols for vectors and their magnitudes (e.g., v, |v|, ||v||, v).

AD5F9185A4D64FECAD5133BBCEC0B29B.description: Represent and model with vector quantities.

BD5CC3AAFD424775A3A9C850C5C7E47F.description: (+) Know the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; show that it is true for quadratic polynomials.

comments: For example, rewrite x² + 4 as (x + 2i)(x - 2i).
B96A3D77FC3643239973A429B000DA50.description: (+) Extend polynomial identities to the complex numbers.

8BCD82F0AE4E499CA6C93B3ACC587AD2.description: Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions.

D62FB173C09A45C5BD85400729621191.description: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.

286BC08F5E624093AFA7E4FBF4062D5C.description: (+) Calculate the distance between numbers in the complex plane as the modulus of the difference, and the midpoint of a segment as the average of the numbers at its endpoints.

D5A17BE595574D709EC46601DC9607A7.description: (+) Represent addition, subtraction, multiplication, and conjugation of complex numbers geometrically on the complex plane; use properties of this representation for computation.
comments: For example, (-1 + √3 i)³ = 8 because (-1 + √3 i) has modulus 2 and argument 120°.

E580F9CBD57246779349DC68E6E07A51.description: (+) Represent complex numbers on the complex plane in rectangular and polar form (including real and imaginary numbers), and explain why the rectangular and polar forms of a given complex number represent the same number.

ACF518D434D54E04B97514A8935D2A4D.description: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.

C4087BDA05824665A600E37ABFAA4D59.description: (+) Find the conjugate of a complex number; use conjugates to find moduli and quotients of complex numbers.

427FF3AF571B46CABD2A685A857D719F.description: Use the relation i² = -1 and the commutative, associative, and distributive properties to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.

8245D55A8D8249E2A60ED9B0A851E8CA.description: Know there is a complex number i such that i² = -1, and every complex number has the form a + bi with a and b real.

E7412D7EFB6445FA8432975C2B10C772.description: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.

A0324DCF5221482A8D86247B9B274448.description: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.

7E16D9100BAE4EA69A7212C92FC5A7C7.description: Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.

DC66BF33621049E9A8A1EAD3A7A82130.description: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.

E21169A8DF0744978B482F2DA9DD4892.description: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

132DF233AFCD4A9A84A86614E9FFD6A7.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

AA547BB6EC19412BA6BBCBE5372FD665.description: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.

28856966A11D4F38A4A4308C467E8459.description: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

256662617EDB43B2B81226B25D212E6E.description: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents.
comments: For example, we define 5<sup>1/3</sup> to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ = 5(<sup>1/3</sup>)³ to hold, so (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ must equal 5.

DB830241B6754EAFA8AEFCFC68B591AD.description: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.

39CAC6EBA1EF44A583B751098C612FD1.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
BB67C7BB964A460B90D96AE4C156A512.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
0A815E849D6C41A6A6358B029D369DFC.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

939A228898814BC197614B1C9584A37A.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New Mexico Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

C33AB4BC30E64B369F264BEFF190CEE2.description: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
comments: For example, "Can you join these two triangles with full sides touching to make a rectangle?"

F361BCF5054444CEA31AF558CC8729A4.description: Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls) and drawing shapes.

A0ECF56A73A848ED92F6C1E14C1B7255.description: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/"corners") and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).

BA519DB7275742259A98CB24CA937298.description: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.

6D4354B285574DCAA896505271321F28.description: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, "flat") or three-dimensional ("solid").

15A45AC924894E5A9271A609DF8C3DAD.description: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.

FB051F0D9B804CEDAAD8243C3000A192.description: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

98B1F52EA77F4EFB968E928A124C48DC.description: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).

1DD04EEB00204C1A927D291A26FB0276.description: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
comments: Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.

A90BCA49FCBA4850906C419EE100F0BA.description: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.

comments: For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.
2F27D7E031FD410895B234A005170E30.description: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of"/"less of" the attribute, and describe the difference.

610A807435C04DBCB3C3760F103C514B.description: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

82A12776E9EA47D0A045AB0A37A17E23.description: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

0DE3996B03EE437E96181176CF40C2B5.description: Work with numbers 11—19 to gain foundations for place value.

D272083B53024AF6B54FA8718CBF3250.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

B7B3CF9AF2EA4A04ADBFC0F823C2034B.description: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.

F66590BCDEDA4CB588BAC1E9505BF520.description: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).

F02806DA06694BF6A46E50D45FB70C47.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.

1B321C8427B341B994A176D1AA1A20E4.description: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
comments: Drawings need not show details, but should show the mathematics in the problem (This applies wherever drawings are mentioned in the Standards.)

26209EFF49C64FBD851012697659E55F.description: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.

D398714A10EB414AB0688A63BC8E4BDF.description: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

comments: Include groups with up to ten objects.
58F298FE22614CF783F03B6E129D2D4D.description: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.

25C4C2921D9748C69D48DDA9DD998CA8.description: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1—20, count out that many objects.

2A16C9B40C59484A9EEF08BD4B6DCF98.description: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

1438B32919F84EF5AF3BE6582E907B23.description: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

92CEE93BCC9F426E8554358CBAFCD9CE.description: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.

81344A2F0BD149229177510527A5FA29.description: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.

40765F4CD7F8451DB27C523BF1B64531.description: Count to tell the number of objects.

2499E97B19BB425A8395DE4876FC94D7.description: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).

FD0CFB837057441793C01C34D537DBA6.description: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

59B57B0B17164866A657F1C2592B771B.description: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

6C1CD93DAE9B4901B0256AA7BB2C9554.description: Know number names and the count sequence.

document.title: New Mexico Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts

E58F76D46A3C448092B64FBD17BE5263.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using frequently occurring conjunctions to signal simple relationships (e.g., because).

D65F5B72F13F42CFA9932207314E712E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs differing in manner (e.g., look, peek, glance, stare, glare, scowl) and adjectives differing in intensity (e.g., large, gigantic) by defining or choosing them or by acting out the meanings.

FF0FED3073CF49C88146C99169A838FE.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., note places at home that are cozy).

FCE94560B221445E962A4C1156B82FB0.description: Define words by category and by one or more key attributes (e.g., a duck is a bird that swims; a tiger is a large cat with stripes).

722DFE8A262142DAAA1966BA3937AF9A.description: Sort words into categories (e.g., colors, clothing) to gain a sense of the concepts the categories represent.

D0742C7A42174C39AC386793D997092C.description: With guidance and support from adults, demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

C81E0DEFC4A342389EB957497D16DCFA.description: Identify frequently occurring root words (e.g., look) and their inflectional forms (e.g., looks, looked, looking).

AE49E57633164539A9B57272EBF277EF.description: Use frequently occurring affixes as a clue to the meaning of a word.

577F75413BBB4A71BBD3FE3A5D59FA27.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

655DA1C1347A40EFBF1C89F816D426A1.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 1 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.

A08EDD63A25B456FBA12DCB5C324F68E.description: Spell untaught words phonetically, drawing on phonemic awareness and spelling conventions.

1C8D096C98124579A4A6D88E3F1159DE.description: Use conventional spelling for words with common spelling patterns and for frequently occurring irregular words.

D021AC9B65AB4F75A16571D97FFBA62C.description: Use commas in dates and to separate single words in a series.

9F14F54B31CA46E5BDC8FFDF93450742.description: Capitalize dates and names of people.

644CEA30A86A47A8AAEAA619D67CA0E0.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

840C469A15884ACAAAB69CFA5075A2C5.description: Produce and expand complete simple and compound declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts.

7984C12C27D040488E5EAA697AE53E86.description: Use frequently occurring prepositions (e.g., during, beyond, toward).

46E7132738C5498E8C7E2A7902045D7A.description: Use frequently occurring conjunctions (e.g., and, but, or, so, because).

5C50DE5BAB3C466A896545BDCFF8296D.description: Use verbs to convey a sense of past, present, and future (e.g., Yesterday I walked home; Today I walk home; Tomorrow I will walk home).

6FEE29015DE9449EA41947C3D3B1DEEC.description: Use personal, possessive, and indefinite pronouns (e.g., I, me, my; they, them, their; anyone, everything).
